info.headline: Say one clear sentence: short, framed spoken responses about familiar topics.
info.summary: Level A speakers produce short, complete spoken sentences about familiar school and personal topics, leaning heavily on sentence frames, word banks, and visual supports. Tasks center on naming, describing what they see, stating a simple opinion with a reason, and retelling in order. Success means one clear idea spoken in a complete sentence, often rehearsed before delivery.
info.distinguishes: Level A responses are 1–2 short sentences built directly from a provided frame, using everyday and high-frequency academic words and concrete, picture-supported prompts. Speakers rely on frames and choral rehearsal and are not yet expected to connect multiple ideas, add transitions, or justify with evidence — that independence and extended, cohesive discourse is the Level B step up.
canDo: I can name objects and people in a familiar picture using words and short phrases.
I can say one complete sentence using a sentence frame.
I can state a preference or opinion and give one reason with because.
I can retell two or three steps in order using sequence words.
I can use polite social phrases to greet, introduce, and ask for help.
I can compare two familiar pictures using same and different.

info.headline: Connect, justify, and present: extended spoken responses with academic language.
info.summary: Level B speakers produce connected, multi-sentence spoken responses that compare, justify, explain processes, and present information. They use academic transitions, content vocabulary, and discussion moves to support opinions with evidence and respond to peers. Frames now scaffold cohesion and organization rather than single sentences, and independence and extended discourse are the expectation.
info.distinguishes: Compared with Level A, Level B responses are extended and cohesive (multiple connected sentences) and require justification with evidence, academic transitions, and content vocabulary. Speakers compare and contrast, explain multi-step processes, build on classmates' ideas, and deliver short organized presentations — using frames to manage organization and register rather than to produce a single sentence.

C.studentGoal: I can argue, explain, compare, and summarize out loud with evidence and academic language.
C.objective: I can organize an extended spoken response with a clear claim, evidence, and precise vocabulary.
C.target: Today I will practice arguing with evidence, explaining a process, comparing sources and data, and summarizing.
C.teacherSummary: Built for grades 6-8 multilingual learners near exit (about 4.0-4.5). Many are long-term ELs whose speaking lags their listening, so tasks push for extended, organized, academic talk, with three sample answers (A, B, C) that show what growth sounds like.

info.headline: Speak like an expert: argue, explain, compare, and summarize with evidence.
info.summary: Level C speakers give extended, well-organized responses on academic topics. They argue a position with evidence and answer a counterclaim, explain a process from a diagram, compare two sources or two graphs, and summarize a text in their own words. Each task includes three sample answers so students can hear how a response grows from simple to fully developed, and frames focus on precise vocabulary and complex sentences rather than basic structure.
info.distinguishes: Compared with Level B, Level C responses are longer (6-10 connected sentences), use specific evidence such as numbers and quotations, include complex sentences with although, which, and as a result, and require synthesis: combining two sources, interpreting data, or responding to an opposing view. Speakers adjust register for a formal audience.
canDo: I can argue a position with specific evidence and respond to a counterclaim.
I can explain a multi-step process from a diagram using sequence and cause-effect language.
I can compare two graphs or sources and explain what they show together.
I can summarize a text in my own words with the main idea and key details.
I can explain my reasoning for a math or science problem step by step.
I can build on a classmate's idea in an academic discussion.

Comparing and synthesizing sources and data

activities.title: Argue: Should Our School Install Solar Panels?
activities.skill: Arguing a position with data as evidence
activities.directions: Study the bar graph about a school's electricity use. Then speak 6-8 sentences: state a claim, use two numbers from the graph as evidence, explain your reasoning, and finish with a conclusion.
activities.prompt: Should our school install solar panels on the roof? Use the bar graph as evidence for your position.

chart.title: Lincoln Middle School: Electricity Used per Month

activities.responsePlaceholder: Claim: ___ / Evidence 1: ___ / Evidence 2: ___ / Reasoning: ___
sayFor: reasoning that connects the numbers to your claim

models.A: The school should get solar panels. The school uses a lot of electricity. In December it is 58. Solar panels make electricity. So it is good.
models.B: I think our school should install solar panels. The graph shows the school uses a lot of electricity every month. For example, it used 58 thousand kilowatt-hours in December and 55 thousand in June. Solar panels can make some of that electricity from the sun. This would help the school save money. In conclusion, solar panels are a good idea.
models.C: I strongly believe our school should install solar panels on the roof. According to the bar graph, the school uses between 42 and 58 thousand kilowatt-hours of electricity every month, with the highest use in December. Even in June, when days are longest, the school still used 55 thousand. Because solar panels produce the most power in late spring and summer, they could cover a large share of our use in May and June, which would lower the electric bill. Although the panels cost money at first, the savings would continue for many years. Therefore, solar panels are a smart investment for both our budget and the environment.

activities.title: Summarize Aloud: Why Cities Are Hotter

activities.prompt: Summarize the article "Urban Heat Islands" in your own words.
passage: On a summer afternoon, a city can be as much as 7 degrees Fahrenheit hotter than the countryside around it. Scientists call this an urban heat island.

The main cause is the materials cities are built from. Dark asphalt roads and roofs absorb sunlight during the day and release that heat slowly at night, so neighborhoods never fully cool down. Cities also have fewer trees, which normally cool the air by providing shade and releasing water vapor from their leaves.
Heat islands are more than uncomfortable. They raise electricity use for air conditioning and can be dangerous for older adults and young children during heat waves.
Cities are fighting back. Some are painting roofs white to reflect sunlight, and others are planting thousands of street trees in the hottest neighborhoods first.

This happens mainly because dark asphalt and roofs absorb heat during the day and release it at night, and because cities have fewer trees to provide shade. activities.prompt: Why did the two hillsides change so differently after the storm? Explain the causes and effects.
